Now Open: From Remote Communities to Your Plate, This New Online Marketplace Delivers Indigenous-Owned, Wild-Harvested Ingredients

Bringing diners across the country closer to Australia's most remote ingredients, this new marketplace already has acclaimed fans, including Melbourne fine-diner Attica.
Hudson Brown
Published on September 02, 2026
Show all photos
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:47
Instaread

Whether you're cooking at home or dining at a local restaurant, knowing where your food comes from matters more than ever. Sometimes, that means choosing locally grown veggies or researching the farm behind the ingredients on your plate. Yet a new Indigenous-owned online marketplace is offering an exclusive taste of something wilder, where the people who most understand the land benefit from its bounty.

Just launched, Wild Foods now supplies customers and wholesalers in Brisbane with a selection of wild food products gathered by remote Indigenous-owned producers. To start, the marketplace features products from Bush Beef and Salty Monkeys Seafood — two standout First Nations suppliers based in Northern Australia — bringing ethically caught, responsibly farmed and Indigenous-owned flavours to the table.

With every product available on the marketplace wild-harvested — not farmed or feedlot-raised — Bush Beef makes for the perfect debut supplier. Operating from Normanby Aboriginal Corporation on Balnggarrawarra Country in Cape York, the station's cattle graze on open savannah grasses, resulting in small-batch products like wild beef mince, wild beef pies and specialty cuts for restaurants.

Meanwhile, hailing from Badu and Thursday Island in the Torres Strait, Salty Monkeys Seafood provides the Wild Foods marketplace with fresh tropical rock lobster, known as kaiar. Hand-caught by local free-divers in partnership with the region's Traditional Owners, kaiar is one of the most sustainable options for local lobster available. Straight from the reef, this is seafood with provenance you'll be keen to learn more about.

Adding some serious culinary credence to the fledgling marketplace, one of Australia's most acclaimed restaurants is already on board, with Melbourne fine-diner Attica now serving Bush Beef. "We're always looking for delicious, unique, and sustainable ingredients to add to our menu," says renowned Attica chef-owner Ben Shewry. "This food is harvested with respect for the planet, and we are proud to cook and serve it."

With plans to expand to Sydney within months, followed by the rest of Australia, Wild Foods offers a direct-to-market supply chain for First Nations producers, complete with cold chain logistics, food safety compliance, marketing and market access that would otherwise be cost-prohibitive for small and remote operators. That's not only good for far-flung businesses; it also unites customers who care about each bite with our fascinating Indigenous food ecosystem.

Orders are now available for customers in Brisbane, with more states to follow. Head to the website for more information.

The Naked Baker - Marrickville

Mortdale's standout bakery-cafe has expanded to Marrickville, with croffles, chorizo eggs and a miso caramel apple turnover on the menu.
Hudson Brown
Published on October 09, 2026
Updated on October 12, 2026

Overview

Since opening in 2023, The Naked Baker has been one of South Sydney's standout cafes, playing a major role in Mortdale's community vibe. As word of its maple croffle eggs benedict and chorizo eggs spreads around town, a second location has officially opened in Marrickville. 

While the brand has made its name on baked goods and classic brekky dishes, which all make the move north, the team is also putting out a new signature dish for the store's grand opening: a humble apple turnover, complete with miso caramel apple, nutmeg custard and flaky layers of croissant-laminated pastry.

"I wanted to create something that tasted nostalgic," says The Naked Baker owner Dino Manoleskos, with the classic sweet treat a childhood favourite of his. "We've also developed two specialty drinks just for Marrickville, a Vietnamese salted cold foam latte and a blueberry matcha."

On the corner of Addison Road and Fotheringham Lane, the new location offers an expansive, industrial space with capacity for 100 seated guests. Like the Mortdale original, Manoleskos wants customers to see the venue less as a pure bakery and more as a top-notch cafe that bakes, with everything from focaccia to Portuguese tarts made in-house. 

"I couldn't believe my luck when this space was available," he says. "We've also tried to create more of a restaurant-style feel, with nice crockery and stone tables, so guests can feel comfortable to stay for as long as they want."

Like the Mortdale store, the kitchen in the Marrickville location is encased in glass, giving customers a front-row view of the baking happening inside - hence the name. Meanwhile, an extensive cream bench lined with glass cabinets greets customers with the day's delicacies as they step inside.
